newsitem.title: GERMANY: Veba, RWE forge ahead after C&W.
newsitem.headline: Veba, RWE forge ahead after C&W.

text.p: German utilities Veba AG and RWE AG on Friday forged ahead with a domestic telecommunications alliance after confirming the long-expected departure of Cable and Wireless from the venture.

The loss of Britain's C&W leaves the German venture without an international partner, which industry analysts said could slow down the group's efforts to become a serious challenger to incumbent monopoly Deutsche Telekom.
The German Cartel Office in Berlin approved the domestic joint venture, to be called O.TEL.O, after it became clear that C&W would leave the alliance.

Veba has agreed to pay C&W about 2.21 billion marks ($1.3 billion) for C&W's 45 percent stake in the Vebacom phone venture they formed two years ago. RWE joined the alliance last October, but had no equity in the group because final contracts were not signed.

Veba chief Ulrich Hartmann, in an apparent reference to C&W's reluctance to step up investment in telecommunications infrastructure in Germany, shrugged off the company's departure and said Veba and RWE were looking for a new partner.
"For our aggressive market strategy in Germany we need partners who can maintain our tempo," he said in a statement.
"With RWE we have found a team-mate who will work with the same strength and commitment towards our demanding goals."

RWE CEO Dietmar Kuhnt said he was sure that the alliance would win a strong position on the German telecommunications market. "With Veba we will seize the chance presented by telecommunications -- the market of the future."

Veba would own 40 percent of O.TEL.O and RWE 37.5 percent. The remaining 22.5 percent made available by the withdrawal of Cable & Wireless will be held in trust by a bank while a new international partner is sought.

The new company already serves over two million customers in Germany, including 700 large customers, over 500,000 mobile phone users -- on the E-plus network in which Veba owns 30 percent -- and 1.6 million cable TV subscribers.

The 2,100 workers at O.TEL.O have already begun their work. Veba will bring the activities of Vebacom and RWE's its unit Telliance -- with the exception of Talkline -- into the new joint venture's operating structure.

O.TEL.O chief executive will be former Vebacom head Ulf Bohla. The company will offer fixed-line networks for business and private customers, mobile phone and paging services, data transfer and multimedia services and cable television.
Industry analysts were concerned about C&W's departure from the group so close to January 1, 1998, when the final barriers to full competition in the European telecommunications sector fall.

They said the departure deprives the utilities' telecom venture of access to international markets and leaves them scrambling to build up a phone network for Germany's liberalised market with little experience in the business.

"We were always pessimistic about Veba's alliance and we still are," said a financial analyst in Frankfurt who follows the utilities. "They don't have a large network and have little to offer without a strong partner."
